The leading semiconductor foundry has fallen with the wider artificial intelligence (AI) trade. Shares are down roughly 26% since hitting an early-October peak of $487, pulled down by a semiconductor sell-off triggered by leadership turmoil at Nvidia (NVDA) and fresh U.S. export curbs. On the company's third-quarter earnings call in October, CEO C.C. Wei said, "demand for our leading-edge technologies continues to be extremely robust." The company's October 2026 revenue also grew 59.7% year-over-year. While AI spending could disappoint, and China restrictions carry real consequences, TSMC's customers still need more advanced manufacturing capacity than it can supply. At about 15.38x next year's earnings, I think the sell-off offers an attractive entry point. I therefore rate TSM stock a Buy. Investors are questioning whether hyperscalers will earn adequate returns on enormous infrastructure spending. Nvidia's leadership turmoil has intensified uncertainty around its China business. The announcement from Washington earlier this week adds tougher foundry-customer checks and restrictions targeting China's remote access to advanced AI computing. Those developments can remove potential orders. Nvidia is a major customer, and a broader spending slowdown would affect TSMC. Its customer diversity doesn't protect it from an industry-wide retrenchment. Rather, it provides exposure across competing chip designs. Nvidia could lose some accelerator share while AMD (AMD) gains it. Both companies rely on TSMC for advanced manufacturing. Google (GOOGL) and Amazon's (AMZN) custom accelerators provide other routes for AI spending to reach the foundry. Broadcom's (AVGO) designs are another example. Its latest quarterly filing says TSMC produced roughly 95% of wafers supplied by its contract manufacturers during the first nine months. So changing winners among chip designers needn't mean fewer orders for TSMC. That distinction is central to my thesis. Customers can compete fiercely over AI profits while continuing to buy manufacturing services from the same supplier. TSMC's process expertise makes switching difficult. Its enormous scale also helps spread development costs across a broad customer base. Building another leading-edge factory takes years, and matching its yields is a separate challenge. I think the market is applying too much of chip designers' uncertainty to the company that manufactures their products. TSMC's October revenue strengthens the growth case after an already excellent Q3. Quarterly revenue rose 50.9% in Taiwan dollars, while net income increased 68.7%. Gross margin reached 66.4%, and 2nm contributed 8% of wafer revenue. Then last week's monthly report showed record October revenue of NT$586.9 billion (about $17.8 billion). That was up 14.7% sequentially and 59.7% year-over-year. Revenue through October increased 43.3%. Growth accelerated after Q3, using the same local-currency comparison. That's difficult to reconcile with the idea that demand is already weakening materially. Management's Q4 revenue guidance of $52.3 billion–$54.3 billion comes with 65%–67% gross margins. The steep 2nm ramp should help. More revealing, though, is the spending commitment beyond this quarter. TSMC expects $60 billion–$64 billion of capex in 2026, and management indicated that total investment over 2026–2028 should significantly exceed the previous three years. Since leading-edge capacity takes years to bring online, customers plan capacity alongside TSMC well in advance. Management has even sent teams to check U.S. data center construction and power availability. Capex doesn't guarantee future sales, but collaborative capacity planning gives these investment figures far more weight than an optimistic forecast alone. The 2nm family's annual capacity should more than double in 2027. A16 expands its high-performance computing offering, while A14 volume production is planned for 2028. Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate (CoWoS) packaging remains another scarce capability needed to assemble advanced AI systems. Agentic workloads are increasing demand for central processing units (CPUs), alongside inference accelerators and networking chips. Smartphones also support adoption of advanced processes. Overseas expansion, including Arizona's next fab in 2027, adds capacity across more locations. So I see a manufacturing franchise expanding around several sources of demand, with customers already planning subsequent product generations. TSMC's valuation leaves room for excellent returns if earnings follow current expectations. At today's price, consensus 2026 earnings per share (EPS) of $17.50 implies 20.55x earnings. The $23.39 estimate for 2027 reduces that to 15.38x. By 2028, $29.82 of EPS implies just 12.06x. Those forecasts assume roughly 34% earnings growth next year and 27.5% afterward. This is an unusually modest price for this growth profile. The opportunity has historical context. Forward P/E fell near 12x–13x in late 2022 and roughly 15x during parts of 2023. Patient buyers eventually benefited as earnings recovered and the shares rerated. I use that comparison cautiously. Still, today's business is growing rapidly, with October revenue 59.7% higher. The technology position remains strong, and new capacity is being planned against customer demand. That makes a compressed multiple particularly interesting to me. Customer concentration and Taiwan's geopolitical risks deserve a valuation discount. Export restrictions could tighten further, and enormous capex creates financial exposure if demand slows. Overseas fabs can also pressure margins. Eventually, leading-edge supply could catch up. Still, even 16x the 2028 EPS estimate would imply roughly $477 per share before dividends. That illustrates why the return case can work without an extreme valuation. Further estimate increases would provide additional upside. Wall Street therefore remains optimistic despite the recent deterioration in semiconductor sentiment. TSMC will feel any genuine slowdown in AI investment. Yet its latest revenue figures show customers still demanding more leading-edge capacity. It can benefit as competing chip designers expand, even as market shares shift. At about 15.38x 2027 earnings, I think that position is attractively priced. October's revenue acceleration gives me more confidence in buying the decline. title: 3 Arizona Towns That Vanished Without a Trace - k101sv.com
content: Arizona is home to hundreds of ghost towns, each with a story of ambition, prosperity, and sudden decline. Built during mining booms, frontier expansion, and the rise of automobile travel, these communities once thrived before changing fortunes left them abandoned to the desert. From booming mine camps to Route 66 tourist attractions, here are 3 Arizona Towns that no longer exist. Vulture City was founded in 1863 after prospector Henry Wickenburg uncovered a massive gold deposit nearby. The find led to the Vulture Mine, once considered the most prosperous gold mine in the state. As news of the strike quickly spread, Vulture City was developed and soon grew to roughly 5,000 residents. Despite its prosperity, Vulture City endured severe hardship, including a deadly dam collapse in 1890, a theft-related mine collapse in 1923, and dozens of executions at its infamous Hanging Tree. The final blow arrived in 1942 when a World War II federal order shut down non-essential gold mining. With the center of the town's economy gone, residents left overnight. Today, Vulture City stands completely abandoned, with no permanent residents or functioning businesses. However, instead of disappearing into the desert, the town was restored and now operates as an open-air museum you can visit! READ MORE ON VULTURE CITY: Rise and Fall of Vulture City, Arizona Unlike most Arizona ghost towns, Two Guns wasn't built around a mine. It began as a small roadside stop along Route 66, at the edge of Canyon Diablo, with only a gas station, a trading post, and a small restaurant. In 1925, entrepreneur Henry E. Miller leased the property and turned it into a popular roadside stop, complete with gift shops, a zoo, sightseeing, and tours of the infamous Apache Death Cave. As automobile travel in the Southwest boomed, Two Guns quickly became one of the most popular stops along Route 66. By the 1970s, the once-popular tourist town had been completely abandoned. Ownership disputes stalled development, fires destroyed several businesses, and interstate construction diverted travellers away from the town. Today, little remains of Two Guns besides crumbling stone buildings, rusted animal pens, and graffiti-covered ruins scattered across the desert. RELATED: Two Guns Arizona: History of a Route 66 Ghost Town Charleston emerged in 1879 during Tombstone's silver boom, serving as a supply hub for the region's rapidly growing mining industry. Located along the San Pedro River, the town quickly developed into a thriving commercial center, providing nearby mining camps with lumber, grain, livestock, and other essential goods. At its peak, Charleston was home to several hundred residents and featured hotels, restaurants, saloons, and a thriving business district. The town was also home to a major silver mill that processed ore from Tombstone's mines, helping establish Charleston as one of southeastern Arizona's most important communities. Charleston's decline began in the 1880s as a series of setbacks struck the region. A powerful earthquake damaged buildings throughout southeastern Arizona, while flooding in nearby Tombstone mines crippled silver production and weakened the local economy. Residents gradually left in search of new opportunities, and by the end of the decade the town had been abandoned. Today, little remains beyond scattered foundations and archaeological remnants hidden along the San Pedro River, marking the site of a town that no longer exists. READ MORE: How Ed Shefflin Discovered Silver And Founded Tombstone Arizona's ghost towns may be quiet today, but their stories are far from forgotten. From gold strikes and silver booms to the glory days of Route 66, each of these towns left its mark on the state's history. The people may be gone, but the echoes of these once-thriving communities still linger in the dust. title: Which Town In Cochise County is Growing Fastest? - k101sv.com
content: I've lived in Cochise County for more than 30 years, and I've seen this area expand and change. When I first got here, things moved slowly. There were fewer people than in most of the places I'd lived in the previous 10 years. In Sierra Vista, most of the businesses were concentrated near the gates of Fort Huachuca. In the last 10 or so years, things have changed a lot. Roads have gotten more crowded and busy, and there’s been a lot of expansion with homes and business development. We're not exactly turning into Phoenix; recent studies show that we’ve experienced a lot of growth as Cochise County communities are steadily adding residents. According to the Arizona Office of Economic Opportunity, Cochise County's population reached an estimated 129,042 residents in 2025. This is up 2.6% from 2020. In Cochise County’s incorporated communities, here are the cities that have grown the fastest: Most of the growth in Cochise County is centered in and around Benson and Sierra Vista. Both towns have a lot to offer, and home prices are more affordable than in Arizona's larger metropolitan areas, like Tucson and Phoenix. The largest employer in Cochise County, Fort Huachuca, keeps residents nearby in Sierra Vista and the surrounding areas. There’s also a lot of access to outdoor recreation, and the slower pace attracts retirees, snowbirds, remote workers, military families, and anyone looking to escape big-city traffic. The county's unincorporated areas have also grown by 5.8% between 2020 and 2025, adding nearly 2,730 residents. READ: Where To Get Breakfast In Cochise County, Local Favorites It’s been a slow drip, but the expansion is noticeable. Interestingly, the growth across Cochise County isn’t sudden and dramatic. You don’t see a lot of giant master-planned communities suddenly popping up. Instead, growth seems to happen one neighborhood, one business, or one four-acre plot at a time. After more than three decades living here, I've watched Sierra Vista, Bisbee, Benson, and Huachuca City grow and change, but we're growing at our own pace, and maybe that's not such a bad thing.

According to the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, its interim final rule is scheduled for publication in the Federal Register on November 19, 2026, and takes effect on publication. The rule amends the presumptions that front-end chip fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips, reducing the pathways to overcome them for chip designers located in destinations that face a license requirement. It also requires a license for advanced semiconductors sent to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil. As reported by GuruFocus, TSMC shares were down 4.26% at 10:45 a.m. ET on November 17 as the rule tightened checks on chip foundries. Citing Reuters, GuruFocus said TSMC and Samsung shares also lost ground in Asia because the measure raises due diligence and licensing burdens for foundries serving Chinese fabless companies. Its report carried no comment from TSMC. Per Benzinga, TSMC fell 7.7% over two days of trading in Taipei, as investors watched whether Nvidia will keep financing its customers after Jensen Huang's exit. GuruFocus pointed to TSMC's November revenue report, and any sign of license-related delays, as the next items to watch. title: TSM's $2 Billion Packaging Deal Could Ease a Critical AI Bottleneck - TradingView
content: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited TSM is adding outside manufacturing support to one of the most constrained parts of its artificial intelligence supply chain. A five-year, $2 billion agreement with GlobalFoundries Inc. GFS will establish another source of silicon interposers for TSM’s CoWoS advanced-packaging ecosystem. That matters because back-end capacity remains constrained even as AI-related demand expands. Packaging availability can limit how quickly wafer demand becomes finished product revenue, making added interposer supply strategically important. GlobalFoundries plans to manufacture silicon interposers at its Malta, NY, facility, with volume production expected to begin ramping in the first half of 2028. The agreement gives TSM a U.S.-based source for a component used in advanced packages and provides a framework for future capacity expansion. The arrangement also broadens TSM’s manufacturing support beyond its own facilities. GlobalFoundries said the program is designed to expand capacity over time as customer demand grows, giving the partnership room to scale beyond the initial commitment. CoWoS sits within TSM’s broader 3DFabric portfolio, which combines chip stacking and advanced packaging technologies to connect logic, memory and other components. That integration is increasingly important as customers build larger computing systems that require more components to work together efficiently. Additional interposer supply could eventually help TSM support customers moving toward larger and more complex AI packages. Management said CoWoS remains the leading choice for customers and noted that TSM is already producing packages at five times reticle size while developing larger formats. The deal does not solve the current bottleneck. Qualification work and production execution still need to occur before the planned 2028 volume ramp, leaving near-term back-end constraints in place. TSM has acknowledged a shortage in back-end supply and said demand remains above its current ability to supply. Until outside capacity arrives, revenue conversion will continue to depend on internal expansion, tool conversions, productivity gains and better capacity utilization. Outside manufacturing support adds flexibility to TSM’s broader capacity strategy. Rather than relying on a single source for every packaging component, the company can combine internal expansion with specialized external supply when that helps customers secure enough front-end and back-end capacity. That approach fits management’s wider planning process, which includes checking data-center construction and electricity availability as well as component supply. Amkor Technology, Inc. AMKR is pursuing a similar industry opportunity by expanding its Arizona advanced-packaging and test campus, with planned investment rising to about $12 billion as customer commitments increase. The GlobalFoundries agreement strengthens the long-term packaging capacity story, but execution remains central. The benefit depends on successful qualification, a timely 2028 ramp and TSM’s ability to coordinate wafer output, packaging availability and customer infrastructure readiness. Its Growth Score of B supports the earnings and AI-demand case, while the Value Score of D, Momentum Score of F and VGM Score of D call for greater selectivity. The mix favors investors focused on growth characteristics, but the weaker value and momentum readings temper the near-term setup.
